transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-12-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Scheduled duration: 45 minutes
Participants: Ethan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (CTO, Sparrow Data), Raj Singh (ML Eng), Carmen Li (Head Infra), Ben Torres (FinOps)

Auto Summary: Quick discovery focused on per-token economics across Redwood hosting modes and what a short pilot would look like. Key risk areas: latency SLOs, KV/prefix caching for chat, and data residency/KMS for private deployment.

Topics covered: per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, hosted vs dedicated vs private, pilot scope, security/compliance asks.

--- Transcript (imperfect ASR, timestamps rough) ---
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Olivia, you said you wanted to focus on unit economics and suggested we walk through concrete per-token scenarios for hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[00:10] Olivia (Sparrow): Yeah, hi thanks, uh quick context — Sparrow's building a customer-support summarization pipeline and a realtime assistant for our dashboard. We're expecting variable load, maybe spikes around EOD reports. The finance team wants to understand runway — "how many queries can we run per month" — and what trade offs we should make on latency versus cost.
[00:28] Ethan: Totally. Quick intros — Priya's our SE, she'll go deeper on batching and kv cache, and I will map to pricing and pilot options.
[00:36] Priya (Redwood): Hi folks. One note early: measuring per-token cost without considering batching/caching is misleading. A naive single-request model looks expensive but with proper prefix caching for chat or continuous batching for short inference it drops a lot.
[00:50] Raj (Sparrow): When you say prefix caching, do you mean the KV cache? We tried something in-house but our engineers hit memory explosion at scale.
[00:58] Priya: Right, KV cache yes, apologies sometimes ASR writes K V cache. The difference is storing decoded KV states for recent contexts — keeps compute per token low for subsequent turns. But memory tradeoffs depend on retention window and number of concurrent sessions.
[01:12] Carmen (Sparrow): Our infra constraint: we can't exceed 70% GPU memory or we'll hit OOMs on other workloads. If we do private, we need guarantee on HSM/KMS integration. SOC2 Type II is required for customer contracts.
[01:25] Ben (FinOps): And from budget side we have a Q4-CQ1 runway cap — roughly $60k/month for model infra. We want to model hosted vs dedicated to see where it fits.
[01:35] Ethan: Ok, so I'll give a couple of scenarios: hosted (pay-as-you-go per token with tiered discounts at volume), dedicated (reserved GPU pools, monthly commit), private (license + infra + ops). Each has different fixed vs variable costs.
[01:49] Ethan: For hosted, sample per-token rates vary by model tier, but the key is effective per-inference cost after batching and cached hits. For a short-turn chat scenario with 32-token responses, batching can reduce rounding overhead and KV cache hits can reduce encoder cost.
[02:05] Priya: To make it concrete — if your average QPS is 20 with median response length 40 tokens and you do 2-turn on average, with a 60-second KV retention and reuse rates of 40%, effective cost can drop by ~30-45% vs naive. That's model-dependent.
[02:22] Raj: That 40% reuse number — is that typical?
[02:25] Priya: It's a conservative estimate for interactive assistants with session affinity. For bulk summarization (single shot) reuse is near zero and batching dominates.
[02:33] Ethan: For dedicated, you get better unit economics at scale because reserved capacity drives down per-token GPU overhead and you can use higher batch sizes — though latency SLOs may push different autoscale configs.
[02:44] Olivia: We're very latency sensitive for the dashboard assistant — 95th p95 must be < 300ms ideally. That rules out large batch windows.
[02:53] Priya: Understood. We can configure continuous batching with small max latency (e.g., 10–20ms accrue) or smart front-door routing so critical requests hit low-latency pools. That impacts throughput and costs.
[03:07] Ben: For budgeting I need a simple model: estimated tokens/month, baseline per-token cost, and then a sensitivity for caching/batching.
[03:16] Ethan: We'll send a 3-tier sensitivity table — low/medium/high traffic — with columns for hosted/dedicated/private showing monthly cost, break-even points, and recommendations.
[03:24] Raj: On private — does Redwood support VPC private control plane and on-prem? Our security team is wary of cloud-hosted key material.
[03:31] Priya: Yes we have Redwood Private with customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integration. There's a platform fee and then infra ops. On-prem is also possible but longer lead times.
[03:40] Carmen: Lead time is important. If we opt for private, are we talking weeks or months?
[03:44] Priya: Typical Private onboarding is 6–10 weeks depending on network approvals and certs. Dedicated is usually weeks; hosted is immediate.
[03:50] Olivia: Another question — quantization. Our ML lead wants to reduce costs by running int8 or 4-bit quantized models. Does Redwood recommend certain quant profiles and what impact do they have on latency?
[03:59] Priya: We support several quant profiles; in many cases INT8 gives 2–3x throughput improvements with small quality delta. 4-bit can be great for batch workloads. We'll share model-specific guidance in the benchmark sheet. Note: quantization can reduce memory pressure which helps KV caching.
[04:15] Raj: For SLOs, can we set routing to fallback to a lower-capacity cheaper model if the main model is saturated?
[04:20] Ethan: Yes, smart routing lets you define fallbacks (cheaper model, different region, or dedicated burst). Also you can pin versions and set canary rollouts.
[04:28] Ben: Competitors question: are we likely to be cheaper than OpenAI or Anthropic hosted offerings?
[04:32] Ethan: Depends heavily on your workload shape. For steady high-volume, dedicated or private with quant is often more economical than pay-as-you-go. For spiky low-volume, hosted may be simpler despite higher per-token list price.
[04:43] Carmen: Security checklist — SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, SOC2 report, KMS integration. Can you share docs?
[04:50] Ethan: Yes we'll share our security pack (SOC2 report, infra diagrams, SAML guide, RBAC descriptions).
[04:55] Olivia: For the pilot, what would you recommend? A hosted trial with synthetic traffic then move to a small dedicated pool?
[05:01] Priya: We often run a 4-week hosted pilot with traffic mirroring, collect token counts, cache hit rates, latency distributions, then propose a dedicated footprint once we have real telemetry. That minimizes upfront commit.
[05:12] Raj: For telemetry, what tracing do you expose? Per-route token costs and p95/p99?
[05:17] Priya: Redwood Console gives per-route token/latency breakdowns, traces, and an eval hook so you can tie quality regressions to prompt sets.
[05:24] Ben: Ok please include a simple ROI calc showing break-even of dedicated vs hosted for our $60k/mo cap.
[05:30] Ethan: Will do. We'll include a chart with assumptions: token sizes, QPS, cache reuse, and GPU pricing.
[05:36] Olivia: Anything else we should prepare?
[05:38] Carmen: I'll get our VPC network contacts and KMS owner in the thread.
[05:41] Raj: I'll export a 2-week sample traffic pattern and p95 latency targets.
[05:46] Ethan: Great. Quick recap — next steps: we send pricing scenarios, a benchmark/quantization playbook, security docs; Sparrow sends traffic sample + infra requirements; schedule a technical deep dive next week.
[05:59] Olivia: Sounds good. Thanks.
[06:02] Ethan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials.

--- End Transcript ---
